   - `dependency <service> is stopped`: a service it depends on was stopped on purpose. Start that
     one first, or leave both down.
   - A container that is `dead` or gone counts in `ayeops_reconciler_missing`; the reconciler
     never recreates. `aye deploy`, or `docker compose up -d` in the project, does.
4. Once the containers run, the next pass logs `recovered` and the alert clears. To keep a
   service down for good, put it in the module's `exclude` or give it `restart: "no"` in its
   compose file, and redeploy.

reconciler-stale.name: reconciler-stale
reconciler-stale.text:
# Reconciler stopped checking

`ayeops_reconciler_last_run_timestamp_seconds` on this host is more than 5 minutes old: the
[reconciler](../modules.md#reconciler) has not finished a pass over the declared containers. A
container that goes down now stays down until a person or Docker's own restart policy brings it
back.

## What to do

1. `docker compose ps reconciler` and `docker compose logs --tail 50 reconciler` in the rendered
   project of the host. A pass that could not read Docker logs one line with
   `"event": "error"` and the reason.
2. `docker compose exec -e AYE_RECONCILER_ONCE=1 reconciler python -I /app/reconciler.py` runs
   one pass now and writes the textfile; the alert clears on the next scrape once it succeeds.
3. `permission denied` or `connection refused` on `/var/run/docker.sock`: the socket is not
   reachable as root inside the container, for example a rootless docker with its socket
   elsewhere.
4. The container runs and logs no error, but the metric stays old: the textfile directory is not
   the one node-exporter reads, or node-exporter is down (`target-down`, `host-down`).
5. A pass that hangs: an attempt waits at most `timeout` (2 minutes) for its containers and each
   Docker call at most 30 seconds, so a pass much longer than that points at a daemon that does
   not answer; `docker info` on the host tells.

sentinel-notify-failing.name: sentinel-notify-failing
sentinel-notify-failing.text:
# Sentinel cannot reach Telegram

The last message of the sentinel was not accepted by Telegram. The next time the central host
dies, the sentinel will notice but you will not hear it, except through the dead-man ping.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs sentinel` on the sentinel's host: `telegram_failed` lines carry the
   HTTP status (the token is never logged).
2. `401`: the bot token in `AYE_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` is wrong or was revoked; `400 chat not
   found` or `403`: `AYE_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID` is wrong, or the bot was removed from the chat.
   Compare with the values of the Grafana contact point, which should be the same.
3. A connection error: the sentinel's host cannot reach `api.telegram.org`; check its DNS and
   outbound firewall.
4. After fixing the `.env`, `docker compose up -d sentinel`. The message is retried every round
   until it is delivered, and the alert clears with the next delivered one.

sentinel-ping-failing.name: sentinel-ping-failing
sentinel-ping-failing.text:
# Sentinel dead-man ping failing

For 15 minutes the sentinel could not ping `AYE_SENTINEL_PING_URL`. The dead-man service then
reports the sentinel as down although it runs, and, worse, would not notice if it really died.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs sentinel`: `ping_failed` lines name the error.
2. `ValueError` or `unknown url type`: the variable holds a placeholder such as `replace-me`;
   put the ping URL of the check there (`https://hc-ping.com/<uuid>`) or leave it empty to turn
   the ping off.
3. HTTP 404: the check was deleted or the UUID is mistyped; copy the URL again.
4. A connection error: the host cannot reach the ping service; check its DNS and outbound
   firewall.
5. `docker compose up -d sentinel` after changing the `.env`.

The ping is sent only after a round where every check passed, so while the central host is down
this alert cannot fire anyway: that silence is the dead-man service's job.

sentinel-stalled.name: sentinel-stalled
sentinel-stalled.text:
# Sentinel stopped checking

The sentinel answers scrapes but has not finished a round of checks for 5 minutes, so it would
not notice the central host dying. Its `/health` answers 503 in this state.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs --tail 50 sentinel`: a `round_failed` line shows an error the loop
   survived; no lines at all point to a hung check.
2. `docker compose restart sentinel`.
3. If it stalls again, compare `interval` with the number of checks times `timeout`: a round
   must fit in a few intervals; lower `timeout` or drop a check.
4. Check the host itself: memory (the container is limited to 48 MB), CPU steal on a small VM.

smart-failing.name: smart-failing
smart-failing.text:
# SMART health check failing

The drive's own health self-assessment (`smartctl -H`) reports a failure. The drive predicts
that it will fail; treat its data as at risk now.

## What to do

1. Check that the latest backup of everything on the drive is complete and restorable.
2. `sudo smartctl -a /dev/<device>`: read the failing attributes and the error log.
3. Copy the data off (`ddrescue` for a degraded drive) and replace the drive. On RAID or ZFS,
   replace the member and let it resilver.
4. Do not run long self-tests on a failing drive before the data is safe: they add wear.

smart-sectors-growing.name: smart-sectors-growing
smart-sectors-growing.text:
# Bad sectors or media errors growing

Within the last day the drive reallocated sectors, found new pending or offline-uncorrectable
sectors (SATA), or logged media errors (NVMe). A single event can be benign; a growing count is
the classic early sign of a dying drive.

## What to do

1. `sudo smartctl -a /dev/<device>`: note `Reallocated_Sector_Ct`, `Current_Pending_Sector`,
   `Offline_Uncorrectable` or `Media and Data Integrity Errors`, and compare with the day before.
2. Verify the backups of the drive.
3. Run a long self-test while the drive is idle: `sudo smartctl -t long /dev/<device>`.
4. If the count keeps growing over the next days, plan a replacement.

status-push-failing.name: status-push-failing
status-push-failing.text:
# Status page reporter cannot push

The [status reporter](../modules.md#status) has not had a push accepted by the status page
Worker for 5 minutes. The Worker shows every component that waits for pushes as **no data**
after the same 5 minutes, so the public page has lost the stack's view of them. The alert also
fires when the reporter stopped exporting its metrics at all (no data counts as firing).

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs --tail 20 status-reporter`: each failed round logs one `push_failed`
   line with `reason`, the HTTP `status` and the Worker's answer in `detail`.
2. Go by the reason and status:

| `reason` / `status` | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `refused` / `401` `signature does not verify` | `AYE_STATUS_PUSH_SECRET` differs from the tenant secret in D1, or the tenant has none | set the same value on both sides: `aye status deploy` for D1 ([status.md](../status.md#deploy)), the host's `.env` for the reporter, then `docker compose up -d status-reporter` |
| `refused` / `401` `ts is more than 300 s away` | the host clock is off by more than 5 minutes | `timedatectl status`; enable NTP (`timedatectl set-ntp true`) |
| `refused` / `422` `unknown components` | the manifest has a component the D1 seed does not | run `aye status deploy`, which seeds the components D1 is missing ([status.md](../status.md#deploy)) |
| `refused` / `400` `tenant does not match the hostname` | `status_page.hostname` routes to another tenant | fix the hostname in the manifest or the `tenants` row |
| `refused` / `404` | the hostname does not route to the Worker | the routes `aye status deploy` prints and the custom domain in the Cloudflare dashboard |
| `transient` / `0` | DNS, TLS or the connection failed three times in a row | `docker compose exec status-reporter python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('https://<status hostname>/api/status', timeout=10)"`; outbound HTTPS from the host |
| `transient` / `429` or `5xx` | Cloudflare or the Worker failed | the Worker's logs (`npx wrangler@4.148.0 tail`) and the Workers and D1 free-tier limits in [status.md](../status.md#free-tier-budget) |

3. No `push_failed` lines and no recent lines at all: the loop stalled or the container is
   gone. `docker compose ps status-reporter`, then `docker compose restart status-reporter`.

`ayeops_status_push_failures_total{reason}` counts failed rounds; a `refused` one never heals by
itself, a `transient` one usually does.

status-query-failing.name: status-query-failing
status-query-failing.text:
# Status page reporter cannot read Grafana

The [status reporter](../modules.md#status) has failed to read the alert rules or the silences
from Grafana for 5 minutes. It keeps pushing, but every component it feeds shows **no data** on
the public status page, because without the alerts it cannot tell whether they work.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs status-reporter | grep query_failed`: the `error` names the failure.
2. Go by the error:

| Error | Fix |
|---|---|
| `answered HTTP 401` | Grafana refused the reader token in `/run/grafana-reader/token`, and the file held no newer one when the reporter read it again. The `grafana-reader` service writes a new token on its next pass, within 5 minutes; if `grafana-reader-failing` fires too, follow [that runbook](grafana-reader-failing.md) |
| `answered HTTP 403` | the `Viewer` role of the reader lost a permission, for example after a Grafana upgrade: see [grafana-reader-failing](grafana-reader-failing.md) |
| `cannot read the reader token`, `holds no token` | the `grafana-reader` volume is not mounted or the reader has not written the token yet: `docker compose ps grafana-reader`, then [grafana-reader-failing](grafana-reader-failing.md) |
| `answered HTTP 5xx`, a timeout, `URLError` | Grafana is down or starting: `docker compose ps grafana`, `docker compose logs --tail 50 grafana` |
| `JSONDecodeError` or `the rules answer ...` | Grafana answered something else than its rules API, for example a sign-in page; check that `AYE_STATUS_GRAFANA` is `http://grafana:3000` |

3. Once a read succeeds the log says `query_ok` and the next push carries the real states.

swap-out-sustained.name: swap-out-sustained
swap-out-sustained.text:
# Sustained swap-out

The kernel has been writing more than 256 pages per second (about 1 MiB/s with 4 KiB pages) to
swap for 10 minutes. Available memory can still look fine on such a host: the kernel swaps out
because something keeps asking for more than fits. Large hosts are not immune; a database buffer
pool sized close to the physical memory does exactly this.

## What to do

1. `vmstat 5`: the `so` column confirms the swap-out; `free -h` shows what is left.
2. `ps aux --sort=-rss | head` and `docker stats --no-stream`: who grew.
3. Compare the declared reservations (`reserved`, `mem_limit`) with reality; the `memory-budget`
   rule keeps their sum within 85 % of the host memory.
4. Shrink the biggest consumer (buffer pools, worker counts, caches) or add memory. Lowering
   `vm.swappiness` hides the symptom, not the cause.

target-down.name: target-down
target-down.text:
# Scrape target down

vmagent could not scrape an exporter for 5 minutes. The `job` label names the exporter, `host` the machine.

## What to do

1. `docker compose ps` on the host: is the container running and healthy?
2. `docker compose logs --tail 100 <service>`.
3. If the container restarts in a loop, see [container-restarting](container-restarting.md).
4. If the exporter answers locally but not to vmagent, check the compose network and the scrape target in `vmagent/scrape.yaml`.

tls-expiring.name: tls-expiring
tls-expiring.text:
# TLS certificate expires in less than 14 days

The certificate served at the probed URL expires within 14 days; automatic renewal normally happens at 30.

## What to do

1. Check the renewal logs of whatever issues the certificate (ACME client, CDN, proxy).
2. Renew by hand if needed, then confirm the new expiry on the probes dashboard.

updates-pending-old.name: updates-pending-old
updates-pending-old.text:
# An update has waited for more than 30 days

A dependency of this repository has a newer version released more than 30 days ago that is
still not merged (`ayeops_updates_oldest_pending_release_timestamp_seconds`). The repository
waits 14 days before a version is offered, so its pull request has been open for about two
weeks, or Renovate could not open one.

## What to do

1. Open the repository's dependency dashboard issue: it lists every pending update and why it
   waits (awaiting schedule, pull request limit, pending approval, or an error).
2. Merge the pull request when CI is green, or close it if the version must not be taken:
   Renovate will not reopen a closed pull request for the same version, and the dependency
   drops out of the count after the next run.
3. A major version that needs a migration can be pinned out in the repository's
   `renovate.json` with a `packageRules` entry (`allowedVersions` or `enabled: false`), with the
   reason in its `description`.
4. No pull request at all: the update may be blocked by `prConcurrentLimit`, or the branch
   failed; the run's log in `docker compose logs updates` says which.

updates-stale.name: updates-stale
updates-stale.text:
# No successful dependency update run for 2 days

`ayeops_updates_last_success_timestamp_seconds` on this host is more than two days old: the
daily Renovate run of the [updates](../modules.md#updates) module failed, did not reach every
repository, or did not run. New versions are not turning into pull requests.

An agent that has never succeeded counts from its first start, so a new host stays quiet for two
days.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs --tail 20 updates-agent`: one JSON line per run with `success`,
   `exit_code`, `missing` (repositories absent from the report) and the open and pending counts.
2. `ayeops_updates_last_run_exit_code`: `124` is the `timeout_minutes` limit, `137` the memory
   limit (raise it with `resources`), `1` a Renovate error.
3. `docker compose logs --tail 200 updates | grep -E '"level":(50|60)'` shows Renovate's errors.
   `Bad credentials` or `401` means `AYE_UPDATES_TOKEN` expired or was revoked; `Repository is
   disabled` or a missing repository means the token does not cover it.
4. `docker compose exec -e AYE_UPDATES_ONCE=1 updates-agent python -I /app/updates_agent.py`
   asks for a run now; the alert clears on the next scrape once a run succeeds.
5. `ayeops_updates_last_run_timestamp_seconds` older than a day means the loop is not running:
   `docker compose ps updates updates-agent`.

vulns-critical-fixable.name: vulns-critical-fixable
vulns-critical-fixable.text:
# A running image has a critical vulnerability with a fix

For an hour at least, the last Trivy scan of the [vulns](../modules.md#vulns) module found a
`CRITICAL` vulnerability in an image this host runs, and the advisory names a fixed version of
the package. The fix exists: a newer image, or a rebuild of the same tag on a newer base, would
remove it.

The alert fires once per image. Critical says how bad the flaw is in general, not whether this
container can be reached through it: a vulnerable library the service never loads, or a tool in
the image nobody calls, is still counted.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs --tail 20 vulns-agent`: the JSON line of the last run lists
   `critical_fixable` per image. The counts in PromQL:
   `ayeops_vulns_vulnerabilities{host="<host>", severity="critical", fixed="true"} > 0`.
2. The details are in the report Trivy wrote:
   `docker compose exec vulns-agent cat /state/reports/results` lists the key, exit code and
   image of every scan, and `/state/reports/<key>.json` lists each `VulnerabilityID`,
   `PkgName`, `InstalledVersion` and `FixedVersion` of that image.
3. A pinned image (`grafana/grafana:13.2.3`): look for a newer release that carries the fixed
   package; Renovate's pull request from the [updates](../modules.md#updates) module may already
   be open. An image of the project: rebuild it on a current base image and bump what pins the
   fixed library.
4. Deploy the new image the way the stack is deployed (`aye deploy`, or the project's script).
   The agent asks for a new scan as soon as the list of images it was rendered with changes, so
   the alert resolves within minutes of the deploy, or after the next daily run.
5. When the advisory does not apply and nothing better exists yet, add the image to the module's
   `exclude` with a note in the manifest of why; the image is then not scanned at all.

vulns-scan-failed.name: vulns-scan-failed
vulns-scan-failed.text:
# The vulnerability scan of an image failed

In its last run Trivy of the [vulns](../modules.md#vulns) module wrote no report for this image,
so its vulnerabilities are unknown: the counts of the image are absent, not zero. When every
image of the host fails at once, the vulnerability database did not download.

## What to do

1. `docker compose logs --tail 20 vulns-agent`: `db_update` false means the database step failed,
   `failed` lists the images without a report.
2. `docker compose logs --tail 100 vulns` shows Trivy's own errors. Common ones:
   - `failed to download vulnerability DB`, `TOOMANYREQUESTS` or a timeout: no internet from the
     host, or the registry of the database (`mirror.gcr.io`, then `ghcr.io`) limits this
     address. It clears with the next run.
   - `No such image` and `unauthorized`: the image is not on the host (never pulled, or pruned)
     and the registry refuses an anonymous pull. Pull it on the host, or exclude it.
   - exit code `124` in `/state/reports/results`: the scan took longer than `timeout_minutes`;
     raise it for very large images.
   - exit code `137`: Trivy hit its memory limit; raise it with `resources`.
3. `docker compose ps vulns-proxy`: an unhealthy proxy means Trivy cannot read the local images
   and falls back to the registry.
4. `docker compose exec -e AYE_VULNS_ONCE=1 vulns-agent python -I /app/vulns_agent.py` asks for a
   run now; the loop picks it up within 15 seconds and the alert resolves once the image scans.

vulns-scan-stale.name: vulns-scan-stale
vulns-scan-stale.text:
# No vulnerability scan finished for 2 days

`ayeops_vulns_last_run_timestamp_seconds` on this host is more than two days old: the daily
Trivy run of the [vulns](../modules.md#vulns) module has not finished, good or bad. Nothing is
known about vulnerabilities published since, and the counts on the host are as old as the last
run. Silence here is not a clean result.

An agent that has never run counts from its first start, so a new host stays quiet for two days
unless its first run fails.

## What to do

1. `docker compose ps vulns vulns-agent vulns-proxy`: all three should be running and healthy.
   `vulns` unhealthy means its loop has not touched `/state/loop.alive` for longer than two
   scans; `vulns-agent` unhealthy means the agent loop stopped.
2. `docker compose logs --tail 50 vulns`: a run that hangs on one image stops after
   `timeout_minutes` per image; many large images can make a run long, never two days.
3. `docker compose exec vulns-agent ls -l /state`: a `run.request` that stays means the loop
   does not pick requests up (restart `vulns`); no `run.last` means no run ever finished.
4. `node-exporter` reads the textfile: if it is down, `target-down` fires for it as well and
   this alert follows from it.
5. `docker compose exec -e AYE_VULNS_ONCE=1 vulns-agent python -I /app/vulns_agent.py` asks for a
   run now; the alert resolves on the next scrape after it finishes.

wifi-signal-weak.text:
# Wi-Fi signal below -75 dBm

The Wi-Fi interface has received its access point at less than -75 dBm for 15 minutes. Below
about -70 dBm throughput drops and latency spikes; below -80 dBm connections break.

## What to do

1. `AyeOps / Internet`, row `Link` (`AyeOps / Інтернет`, row `Лінк` with `locale: uk`):
   signal, bitrate and network over the same minutes; on the host, `iw dev <device> link`
   shows the same numbers.
2. Move the host or the access point, prefer 5 GHz for short distances and 2.4 GHz through
   walls, or add a mesh node.
3. For a server, use a cable: Wi-Fi is a link you watch, not one you trust.
